summary.text: Define the comparison sequence by \(c_0=4,c_1=16,c_2=63\) and \(c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\), and prove it is positive with sufficiently rapid growth. For the defects \(\Delta_n=c_{n+1}^2-c_nc_{n+2}\), the identity \(\Delta_{n+3}=4\Delta_{n+1}+\Delta_n\) and the initial values give \(0<\Delta_n\le c_n\); thus \(\lceil c_{n+1}^2/c_n\rceil-1=c_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the original sequence with \(c\) and yields the claimed recurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let \(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer such that
\[
\frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
All terms under consideration will be positive. Multiplying the displayed inequality by the positive number \(b_nb_{n+1}\) shows that an integer \(r\) is admissible precisely when
\[
r<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For any real number \(y\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(y\) is \(\lceil y\rceil-1\), including when \(y\) itself is an integer. Hence the original rule is equivalently
\[
 b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
For positive integers \(u,v\), this ceiling can also be written as
\[
\left\lceil\frac uv\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{u+v-1}{v}\right\rfloor.
\]

We shall prove that the sequence defined by (1) coincides with the integer sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge0}\) defined by
\[
c_0=4,\qquad c_1=16,\qquad c_2=63,
\]
and
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{2}
\]
The main issue is to show that the nonlinear ceiling recurrence (1) always selects the next term prescribed by (2).

First we establish positivity and a useful growth estimate for \(c_n\). We claim that, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
c_n>0,\qquad 3c_n\le c_{n+1},\qquad 3c_{n+1}\le c_{n+2}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=0\), these statements are immediate from
\[
(c_0,c_1,c_2)=(4,16,63):
\]
indeed \(4>0\), \(12\le16\), and \(48\le63\).

Suppose (3) holds at index \(n\). At index \(n+1\), positivity of \(c_{n+1}\) is already part of the induction hypothesis, and the first growth inequality
\(3c_{n+1}\le c_{n+2}\) is also already known. It remains to prove
\[
3c_{n+2}\le c_{n+3}.
\]
By (2),
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n.
\]
The inequalities in (3) imply in particular \(c_n\le c_{n+2}\). Therefore
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\ge 3c_{n+2},
\]
as required. This proves (3) by induction. In particular, every \(c_n\) is a positive integer despite the subtraction in (2).

We next measure how far \(c_{n+1}^2\) lies above \(c_nc_{n+2}\). Define
\[
D_n:=c_{n+1}^2-c_nc_{n+2}. \tag{4}
\]
We will prove
\[
0<D_n\le c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{5}
\]
The first three values are computed directly. From (2),
\[
c_3=4c_2-c_0=4\cdot63-4=248,
\]
and
\[
c_4=4c_3-c_1=4\cdot248-16=976.
\]
Consequently,
\[
D_0=16^2-4\cdot63=256-252=4,
\]
\[
D_1=63^2-16\cdot248=3969-3968=1,
\]
and
\[
D_2=248^2-63\cdot976=61504-61488=16.
\]
Thus
\[
0<D_0=4\le c_0=4,
\]
\[
0<D_1=1\le c_1=16,
\]
and
\[
0<D_2=16\le c_2=63.
\]

The determinants \(D_n\) satisfy a simple recurrence. We claim that
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, by (2),
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n,
\]
\[
c_{n+4}=4c_{n+3}-c_{n+1},
\]
and
\[
c_{n+5}=4c_{n+4}-c_{n+2}.
\]
Substitution into the left side gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{n+3}
 &=c_{n+4}^2-c_{n+3}c_{n+5}\\
 &=c_{n+4}^2-c_{n+3}(4c_{n+4}-c_{n+2})\\
 &=c_{n+4}^2-4c_{n+3}c_{n+4}+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=c_{n+4}(c_{n+4}-4c_{n+3})+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=-c_{n+1}c_{n+4}+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=-c_{n+1}(4c_{n+3}-c_{n+1})+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=c_{n+1}^2+c_{n+3}(c_{n+2}-4c_{n+1})\\
 &=c_{n+1}^2+(4c_{n+2}-c_n)(c_{n+2}-4c_{n+1})\\
 &=c_{n+1}^2-c_nc_{n+2}
   +4(c_{n+2}^2-c_{n+1}c_{n+3})\\
 &=D_n+4D_{n+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (6).

We now prove (5) in blocks of three. Suppose that
\[
0<D_n\le c_n,
\quad 0<D_{n+1}\le c_{n+1},
\quad 0<D_{n+2}\le c_{n+2}.
\]
The last two of these inequalities simply shift forward to provide the first two statements in the next block. For the new third statement, (6) gives
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n>0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
D_{n+3}\le4c_{n+1}+c_n. \tag{7}
\]
We compare this upper bound with \(c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\). From (3),
\[
c_{n+2}\ge3c_{n+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
c_{n+1}\ge3c_n.
\]
Thus
\[
4c_{n+2}-4c_{n+1}-2c_n
\ge 8c_{n+1}-2c_n>0.
\]
In particular,
\[
4c_{n+1}+c_n\le4c_{n+2}-c_n=c_{n+3}. \tag{8}
\]
Combining (7) and (8) yields \(D_{n+3}\le c_{n+3}\). Starting from the already computed cases \(D_0,D_1,D_2\), induction proves (5) for every \(n\).

We can now identify the original sequence \(b_n\) with \(c_n\). We prove simultaneously, by induction on \(n\), that
\[
b_n=c_n\qquad\text{and}\qquad b_{n+1}=c_{n+1}. \tag{9}
\]
For \(n=0\), the first equality is \(b_0=c_0=4\) and the second is \(b_1=c_1=16\).

Assume (9) at index \(n\). By (4) and (5),
\[
1\le c_{n+1}^2-c_nc_{n+2}\le c_n,
\]
where integrality allows us to replace strict positivity by a lower bound of \(1\). Equivalently,
\[
c_nc_{n+2}+1\le c_{n+1}^2\le c_nc_{n+2}+c_n. \tag{10}
\]
Since \(c_n>0\), division by \(c_n\) gives
\[
c_{n+2}<\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}\le c_{n+2}+1. \tag{11}
\]
It follows that
\[
\left\lceil\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}\right\rceil=c_{n+2}+1. \tag{12}
\]
Notice that (12) remains correct when the right inequality in (11) is equality: in that case the fraction is the integer \(c_{n+2}+1\), whose ceiling is itself.

Using the induction hypothesis and the original recurrence (1), we therefore obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+2}
 &=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=\left\lceil\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=c_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the two equalities for the next induction index are \(b_{n+1}=c_{n+1}\), already known, and \(b_{n+2}=c_{n+2}\), just proved. This establishes (9), and hence
\[
b_n=c_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0. \tag{13}
\]

It follows at once from the definition of \(c_n\) that
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n. \tag{14}
\]
Equivalently, for every \(m\ge3\),
\[
b_m=4b_{m-1}-b_{m-3}. \tag{15}
\]
This is an equality of ordinary integers. Its right-hand side is positive because it equals \(b_m\); consequently, if subtraction is interpreted in the nonnegative integers, no truncation occurs. Thus (15) is exactly the claimed recurrence in the original sequence’s natural-number formulation.

For completeness, this recurrence is equivalent to the conjectured generating function. Let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^0\) in \((1-4x+x^3)G(x)\) is
\[
b_0=4.
\]
The coefficient of \(x^1\) is
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,
\]
and that of \(x^2\) is
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For every \(n\ge3\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) is
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3},
\]
which is zero by (15). Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since \(1-4x+x^3\) has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series, and hence
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence produced by the original greatest-integer consecutive-ratio rule satisfies the stated linear recurrence for every index, not merely for the initially observed terms, and its generating function is exactly the conjectured rational function.
